research_insight_text_link.research_insight_description: Saudi Aramco is researching and developing technologies for oil and gas production, including methods for improving oil and gas well productivity, multi-stage sweeping gas membrane distillation systems, integrated flare systems for gas plants, removal of crude oil from water in gas oil separation plants, and estimating molecular weight of hydrocarbons. Additional focus areas include facies clustering for subterranean property modeling, downhole vibration tools, and enhanced hydroprocessing processes with ammonia and carbon dioxide recovery, reflecting a broad approach to energy and gas innovation.

overview_description.description:
The Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Saudi Aramco) is the state-owned oil company of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It ranks first among oil companies worldwide in terms of crude oil production and exports, and natural gas liquids (NGL) exports, and is among the leading producers of natural gas. It is also known as refiners and are moving further downstream into chemicals production.

The company was founded in 1930 and is headquartered in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia.

press_references.value: State-Owned Oil Giants Face Legal Reckoning After ICJ Climate Judgment

legal_proceedings.description: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered a landmark advisory opinion on climate change, clarifying that state-owned oil companies' emissions can be attributed to their home countries under international law, increasing legal risks for companies like Saudi Aramco, Gazprom, Petrobras, Equinor, and ADNOC. This opinion is expected to bolster climate litigation against states and intensify scrutiny of state-owned fossil fuel enterprises.

press_references.value: Fossil fuel companies caused $28 trillion in climate damage, study finds. These 5 are tied to the most harm.

legal_proceedings.description: A Dartmouth College study quantifies climate damage caused by emissions from 111 fossil fuel companies, supporting the scientific basis for climate liability lawsuits against major emitters like Saudi Aramco, Gazprom, Chevron, ExxonMobil, and BP. The study aims to help hold these companies liable for the cost of extreme weather, though no lawsuit has yet succeeded.
